extracted.intended_audience: regulated entities, commenters, environmental and legal stakeholders, and EPA staff involved in CAA section 202(a) rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of the Administrator's statutory and analytical approach for determining whether emissions from new motor vehicles or engines "cause or contribute to" air pollution that may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare under Clean Air Act section 202(a). Describes definitional, evidentiary, and interpretive criteria used in the contribution determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of grouping well-mixed greenhouse gases as a single air pollutant
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator may define a single air pollutant comprised of the well-mixed greenhouse gases (the six gases) based on shared attributes; the reasonableness of this grouping does not turn on the particular source category being evaluated in a contribution finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group substances that share common attributes (e.g., long-lived, well-mixed in the atmosphere, directly emitted, well-known radiative forcing, commonly grouped in climate science/policy fora). EPA analogizes to grouping of VOCs or PM: different sources may emit only a subset of the group, but the group definition remains reasonable. The number of substances in the greenhouse gas group is much smaller than other group pollutants, and defining the group to include substances not emitted by a particular source category does not make the definition unreasonable. Even defining the air pollutant as only the subset emitted by the source category (e.g., four gases) would not materially change the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emissions as a proxy for contribution to atmospheric concentrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using emissions (historical and annual) as a proxy for contributions to atmospheric concentrations is reasonable for well-mixed greenhouse gases because cumulative emissions drive cumulative changes in atmospheric concentrations, and annual emissions proxy annual incremental changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA analyzed historical emissions data (1990–2007) for motor vehicles and engines. The Proposed Findings discussed multiple possible approaches and noted no single approach is required by statute; EPA follows prior cause-or-contribute findings in using emissions as a proxy for contribution to atmospheric concentrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances test in contribution determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator should consider the totality of the circumstances when judging whether emissions from a source category contribute to air pollution, rather than relying on a single numeric threshold or bright line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include the air pollutant, the air pollution, the nature of the endangerment, the type of source category, the number of sources in the source category, and the number and type of other source categories that may emit the air pollutant. Contextual factors (distribution of emissions, number of sources) can change the meaning of a percentage share.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to find a 'significant' contribution or establish a bright-line threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator is not required to set a quantified, uniform amount of contribution (a bright-line or de minimis threshold) below which a source category could never be found to contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent (e.g., Catawba County, Ethyl, Bluewater Network) supports agency discretion; 'contribute' is ambiguous and does not inherently connote magnitude or significance. A contribution may merely exacerbate a problem rather than cause it. EPA need not promulgate pre-specified de minimis guidance to finalize a contribution finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dual comparisons: share of global and share of U.S. aggregate emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess whether CAA section 202(a) source categories contribute to the global greenhouse gas problem, the Administrator used two straightforward comparisons: (1) the source category's share of total current global aggregate emissions of well-mixed greenhouse gases; and (2) the source category's share of total current U.S. aggregate emissions of well-mixed greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both comparisons independently and together support the contribution finding; EPA is not placing primary weight on either approach but finds both approaches clearly establish contribution. Data examples: 2005 global emissions and 2007 U.S. emissions tables are used (see Appendix B of the TSD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual interpretation of percentage comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw percentage shares should not be interpreted in isolation; context (number of sources, distribution of emissions among sources, ranking compared to other emitters) is necessary to evaluate relative impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same percentage can imply different relative importance depending on whether most other sources are larger or smaller. EPA provides examples comparing source-category emissions to entire countries and to U.S. sectors (e.g., electricity generation, transportation) to illustrate context-sensitive interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the global nature of climate change in setting contribution expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because climate change is a global problem with numerous and varied sources, the Administrator may reasonably consider lower percentage levels of emissions as constituting contribution than would be applied in localized or regional air pollution contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The global, well-mixed nature of greenhouse gases means no single country or source dominates the global inventory; successful strategies must address many contributors. EPA analogizes to ozone control where addressing both large and many small sources is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking source category emissions against countries and domestic sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the emissions of the source category to emissions of entire countries and to other U.S. sectors to assess relative importance and inform judgment about contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 2005 CAA section 202(a) share = 4.3% of global GHGs and 28% of global transport GHGs; if ranked against countries, the source category would be behind only China, the U.S. as a whole, Russia, and India. Within the U.S., section 202(a) sources were the second-largest emitter behind electricity generation (2007 data showing 23% share). Such rankings inform the Administrator's view of importance within national strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of air pollutant need not be limited to substances emitted by the specific source category
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator may define the 'air pollutant' to include substances that share attributes even if the specific source category does not emit every substance in the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued PFCs and SF6 should be excluded if not emitted by motor vehicles. EPA responds that grouping by common attributes is reasonable and gives effect to shared attributes; statutes and prior definitions (e.g., VOC, PM) likewise group many substances though single sources may emit only subsets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical emissions inventory and sectoral data as evidentiary basis
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relied on historical emissions inventories and sectoral data (e.g., 1990–2007 U.S. emissions, 2005 global inventory) as the empirical basis for the contribution determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA analyzed trends and sectoral contributions (electricity generation, transportation, industry) and referenced technical support documents (Appendix B of the TSD) and tables (Table 1, Table 2) showing Tg CO2-equivalent values and sectoral shares used in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator's reasoned overall comparison approach rather than exclusive reliance on any single method
rubrics_metrics.description: In making the cause-or-contribute finding, the Administrator focused on a reasoned overall comparison of emissions from the source category to emissions from other sources rather than insisting on one exclusive analytic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the magnitude of emissions and comparisons to other sources were central. EPA noted that different methods have been used in prior determinations and that no single approach is required by the statute; the Administrator's judgment integrates multiple lines of comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on legal precedent for interpretive discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA frames its interpretive approach in light of Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit decisions holding greenhouse gases fit the CAA definition of 'air pollutant' and that 'contribute' is ambiguous, permitting reasonable agency interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases include Massachusetts v. EPA (greenhouse gases are 'air pollutant'), Catawba County v. EPA, Ethyl, and Bluewater Network regarding the meaning of 'contribute' and the absence of a statutory requirement for a quantified contribution threshold. These precedents support EPA's discretion to apply a totality-of-the-circumstances test.
